01.note: Rabban Gamliel was traveling on a ship with other Elders when he remembered he had not tithed the produce of his fields. He declared that the tenth he would later measure out was given to Yehoshua, a Levite, and that the spot where it lay was rented to him. Another tenth, the tithe for the poor, he gave to Akiva ben Yosef to acquire on behalf of the poor, again renting him the place where it lay.
01.why: Ulla holds that a person's field acquires property for him only when he stands next to it. Rabbi Abba objects with this incident: Yehoshua and Akiva were on the ship, far from the field, yet they acquired the tithes. Ulla dismisses the objection.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Raises this incident as an objection to Ulla.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Rabbi Abba challenges.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Travels by ship with other Elders and gives away his tithes while at sea.

people.name: Yehoshua
people.about: Yehoshua ben Hananya, a Levite, who receives the first tithe.

people.name: Akiva ben Yosef
people.about: Receives the poor man's tithe to acquire on behalf of the poor.

terms.meaning: A tenth of a farmer's produce that must be set aside. The first tithe goes to a Levite; in certain years a further tenth, the poor man's tithe, goes to the poor.
Senior Sages and scholars.

02.note: A group of ice plant dealers took turns baking for one another. One day the others asked one of them to bake, and he asked them to watch his cloak. They were careless and it was stolen. Rav Pappa held them liable to pay. The Rabbis objected, since the owner was working for them at the time, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed, until it came out that the owner had in fact been drinking beer, not baking, when the cloak was stolen. The Gemara then retells the case: it was not his turn, and he baked for them in return for their guarding his cloak.
02.why: The discussion has just taught that people who agree to safeguard each other's property count as paid bailees, but that a bailee is exempt when the owner is working for him. This case tests that exemption, and the retelling makes the guards paid bailees.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge who held the guards liable and was embarrassed when challenged.

people.name: The Rabbis
people.about: Challenge Rav Pappa's ruling.

terms.meaning: A rule that a person guarding another's property is exempt from paying if the owner was working for him at the time the guarding began.
Someone who looks after another's property for payment or benefit; he must pay if it is stolen or lost.

03.note: A man rented his donkey to another and warned him not to take the Nehar Pekod road, where there was water, but the Neresh road, where there was none. The renter took the Nehar Pekod road and the donkey died. When he came back he admitted taking that road but said there was no water there. Rava said his word should be accepted, since he could have lied and claimed he took the Neresh road. Abaye answered that this reasoning does not apply where witnesses are available. The text does not say how the case ended.
03.why: It comes in a run of cases about people who used or looked after someone else's property and lost it, such as a stolen cloak and a washed-away sheet. This one asks when a borrower's own account of what happened can be believed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that the renter is believed because he could have told a better lie.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Argues against Rava that the reasoning fails where witnesses can be called.

terms.meaning: A legal principle: if a person could have won with an easier false claim, his actual claim is believed, since a liar would have chosen the better story.

04.note: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi heard that Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, owed his greatness to suffering, he said afflictions must be precious and took thirteen years of them upon himself: kidney stones and scurvy (the Gemara gives two versions of how many years of each). His stableman, said to be richer than the king of Persia, timed the feeding of the animals for when Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi went to the latrine, so their lowing would drown out his screams of pain. Even so, his cries were louder than the animals and were heard by sailors out at sea.
04.why: The Gemara is comparing Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's suffering with Rabbi Elazar's. Right after, it says Rabbi Elazar's afflictions were greater, because they came out of love, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's came and left because of particular incidents.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; takes years of afflictions upon himself.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage whose greatness was said to come from his suffering.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: King of Persia; the stableman is said to be wealthier than he.

terms.meaning: A measure of distance, roughly a kilometer.
A disease of the gums and skin; here one of the two illnesses Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi suffered.

05.note: Visiting the town of the late Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked whether he had a son. He was told the son had gone astray and was hired by prostitutes. He took the young man, ordained him, and gave him to his uncle, Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya, to teach. Each day the young man said he was going home; his uncle shamed him, and he vowed to stay. Grown into a scholar, he sat in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's academy, who recognized his father's voice in his. When this son, Rabbi Yosei, died, a serpent blocked his father's burial cave. A Divine Voice said it was not because the father was greater, but because the father had endured the suffering of the cave and the son had not.
05.why: The Gemara is telling stories of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Elazar. A similar rescue of Rabbi Tarfon's grandson follows, and the Gemara explains why he worked so hard for wayward sons: whoever teaches Torah to another's son earns a place in the heavenly academy.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; brings the wayward son back to Torah study.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The righteous father, already dead; he had suffered in a cave.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's son, who strays and becomes a scholar.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya
people.about: Rabbi Yosei's uncle, his mother's brother, who teaches him.

terms.meaning: Given the title Rabbi; the text describes a golden cloak spread over him.
A voice from Heaven that the Sages describe announcing God's view.
Rabbi Elazar hid in a cave with his father for thirteen years to escape the Romans.

06.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya sent his son to hire workers. The son hired them and promised to feed them, without saying how much. When he came back and told his father, Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya said that even a feast like King Solomon's in his time would not fulfill that promise, because the workers are descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
06.why: The mishna rules that workers' meals follow local custom, but an employer who promises food has added to what he owes. This incident shows how far such an open promise can reach. The Gemara then asks whether Abraham's feast really outdid Solomon's.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya
people.about: The father, who tells his son how much his promise to the workers demands.

people.name: King Solomon
people.about: Mentioned for his lavish feasts.

terms.meaning: The earliest written collection of Jewish law, which the Gemara discusses.

07.note: Rabba bar Rav Huna owned a forest on a riverbank, and people asked him to cut down the trees that blocked the men hauling boats along the bank. He said he would cut his trees once the owners upstream and downstream cut theirs. The Gemara asks how he could wait for others, and answers that the next forest belonged to a Persian general who would ignore a Jewish scholar, so cutting his own would achieve nothing. Rabba bar Rav Nahman sailed by, learned whose forest it was, and ordered it cut down. Rabba bar Rav Huna found it cut and cursed whoever did it: may his branches be cut down. All the years Rabba bar Rav Huna lived, Rabba bar Rav Nahman's children did not survive.
07.why: The Gemara has been discussing how wide a path must be cleared of trees along a river for boat haulers; Rav Natan bar Hoshaya was even beaten for demanding too much. This story shows the rule tested on a Sage's own land.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Owner of the riverside forest, who refuses to cut it alone and curses whoever does.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who orders the forest cut down; his children do not survive.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Quoted by the Gemara: improve yourself first, then others.

people.name: Parzak
people.about: A Persian general whose forest stood beside Rabba bar Rav Huna's.

terms.meaning: Men who walked along the riverbank pulling boats with ropes; trees on the bank got in their way.

08.note: Rav Yosef had a planter working his land who died, leaving five sons-in-law. Rav Yosef reasoned that until now he had dealt with one man, but five would rely on one another and cause him losses. He told them that if they took payment for the improvement they had made to the land and left, well and good; if not, he would remove them with no payment at all. The text does not say what they did.
08.why: It is one of a series of cases about planters leaving a field and whether they are paid for its improvement. Right after, Rav Yosef cites a ruling that a dead planter's heirs can be removed without that payment, and the Gemara says the law does not follow it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A landowner who wants to end his arrangement with his dead planter's heirs.

terms.meaning: A worker who plants and tends trees on another's land in return for a share, like a sharecropper.
The added value a worker's labor has given the land, which he may be owed when he leaves.

09.note: Runya, who planted for Ravina, caused a loss, and Ravina removed him from the field. Runya complained to Rava about what Ravina had done. Rava said Ravina had acted well. Runya protested that Ravina had not warned him first, and Rava replied that no warning was needed.
09.why: The Gemara has been asking whether a planter who causes a loss leaves with or without pay. The Gemara says Rava follows his own rule: teachers of children, planters, slaughterers, bloodletters and scribes count as warned in advance for any loss that cannot be undone.

people.name: Runya
people.about: Ravina's planter, removed for causing a loss.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The landowner who dismisses Runya.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules that Ravina acted rightly.

terms.meaning: A worker who plants and tends trees on another's land, like a sharecropper.

10.note: Ifera Hurmiz, mother of the Persian king Shapur, sent four hundred dinars to Rabbi Ami, who refused them. She sent them to Rava, who accepted them for the sake of peace with the kingdom. Rabbi Ami heard and was angry, citing a verse that the nations should not be helped to do good deeds. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Ami held the money should have gone to the gentile poor, that Rava had in fact given it to them, and that Rabbi Ami was angry only because he had not been told the end of the story.
10.why: The Gemara has been discussing a verse read as saying that the charity of other nations counts against them, while Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai held it atones for them. This story shows two Sages disagreeing over whether to take a gentile queen's charity.

people.name: Ifera Hurmiz
people.about: Mother of King Shapur; sends money for charity.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Refuses her gift and is angry that Rava accepts it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Accepts the gift for the sake of peace with the kingdom.

terms.meaning: A coin.
Keeping good relations with the ruling government, here the Persian crown.

11.note: A relative of Rav Idi bar Avin died and left a date tree. Another man took it, and each claimed to be the closer relative. In the end the man admitted that Rav Idi bar Avin was closer, and Rav Hisda gave him the tree. Rav Idi then asked to be repaid for the dates the man had eaten all along. Rav Hisda mocked him, asking whether this was the man called great: his claim rested on the other man's word, and until his admission that man had said he was closer.
11.why: The Gemara has been weighing when a person's own claim is believed. Here it notes that Abaye and Rava reject Rav Hisda's view: once the man admitted he was not the closer relative, he admitted he never had a right to the dates.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Claims a dead relative's date tree and its fruit.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The judge who gives Rav Idi the tree but refuses repayment for the fruit.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Disagrees with Rav Hisda's ruling.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Disagrees with Rav Hisda's ruling.

12.note: A firstborn son sold both his own share and his dead brother's share of their father's property before it was divided. His brother's orphaned sons went to eat dates from the field, and the buyers beat them. Their relatives protested that the buyers had bought the orphans' property and were now beating them too. The case came before Rava, who said the firstborn had done nothing: the sale was not valid.
12.why: Rav Pappa and Rav Pappi each quote Rava differently on whether a firstborn who takes an ordinary share gives up his extra portion. The Gemara says Rava never ruled on that directly; both views were inferred from this ruling.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules the firstborn's sale void.

terms.meaning: The eldest son, who inherits a double portion of his father's property.
A son who is not the firstborn and receives a single share.

13.note: Rav Zutra bar Toviyya's mother signed her property over to him because she wanted to marry Rav Zevid. She married him, and he divorced her. She came to Rav Beivai bar Abaye to get her property back. He ruled that she had given it so she could marry, and she had married, so the gift stood. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, mocked him for coming from a family of people cut off young, and argued that since she had said the gift was for the sake of the marriage, and she was now divorced, she could take it back.
13.why: The Gemara introduces a series of cases with a short memory aid, starting with this one. All of them concern gifts of property and whether the giver can take them back.

people.name: Rav Zutra bar Toviyya
people.about: The son who received his mother's property.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: The man she married, who divorced her.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: Rules that the gift to her son stands.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Mocks Rav Beivai and argues she can reclaim the property.

terms.meaning: When a woman about to marry writes her property over to someone else so that her husband does not gain rights to it.
An insult: Rav Beivai's family was said to descend from the priest Eli, whose descendants were cursed to die young.

14.note: In Bnei Brak a man sold some of the property he had inherited from his father, and then died. His family contested the sale, saying he had still been a minor when he died, so the sale was invalid. They asked Rabbi Akiva whether they could exhume him to examine the body. He said they were not permitted to disgrace him, and besides, the signs of puberty can change after death.
14.why: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish disagree on how proof must be brought: by witnesses or by confirming the deed. Rabbi Yohanan cites this case against Reish Lakish, and the two argue over who held the property and who was contesting it.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Cites this case as an objection to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: Also called Reish Lakish; the Sage being challenged.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Refuses to let the family exhume the dead man.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna.
Someone under the age of legal adulthood; a sale of inherited land by a minor is not valid.
Physical signs that showed a person had reached legal adulthood.

15.note: A man died owing money, leaving young orphans. His guarantor paid the creditor without first telling the orphans, and then wanted the orphans to repay him. Rav Pappa said that repaying a creditor is a religious duty, and minor orphans are not obligated in such duties. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said that perhaps the father had already handed the creditor bundles of money before he died. By both views the orphans need not repay until they come of age.
15.why: The Gemara has been discussing guarantors and the rule that a creditor cannot collect from a debtor's property before claiming from the debtor. Afterward it asks when Rav Pappa's and Rav Huna's reasons would lead to different rulings.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Says minor orphans need not repay because they are not obligated in religious duties.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Says the father may already have repaid part or all of the debt.

terms.meaning: A person who promises to pay a loan if the borrower does not.
A religious commandment or duty.

16.note: A promissory note turned up in the keeping of a woman, who told the court she knew the debt had been repaid. Rav Nahman believed her. Rava asked whether this followed the view that a note is transferred just by handing it over. Rav Nahman said no: she was believed because she could have burned it. Others tell it the other way: Rav Nahman did not believe her, Rava asked why not, since she could have burned it, and Rav Nahman answered that once a note has been confirmed in court, that argument does not apply.
16.why: The Gemara has been collecting Rav Nahman's rulings on when evidence is accepted in court. Right after, Rava challenges him from a teaching that a third party holding a receipt is believed, and the Gemara declares Rav Nahman's view conclusively refuted.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who decides whether to believe the woman.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Questions Rav Nahman's ruling.

terms.meaning: A written document recording a debt, which a lender can use to collect.
A note whose signatures a court has checked and approved; it cannot be cancelled without evidence.

17.note: Imrata bat Talei was a priest's daughter who committed adultery. Rav Hama bar Toviyya had her surrounded with bundles of branches and burned her.
17.why: The discussion concerns execution by burning, the Torah's penalty for a priest's daughter who commits adultery. Rav Yosef says Rav Hama bar Toviyya erred twice: burning is done another way, and capital cases are not judged when there is no Temple.

people.name: Imrata bat Talei
people.about: A priest's daughter who committed adultery.

people.name: Rav Hama bar Toviyya
people.about: The judge who had her burned.

terms.meaning: The daughter of a priest (kohen); the Torah sets burning as the penalty if she commits adultery.

18.note: The Roman emperor Antoninus told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi he wanted two things: for his son Asveirus to rule after him, and for Tiberias to be freed from taxes. The Roman leaders would grant one request but not two. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi set one man on another's shoulders, gave a dove to the one on top, and told the one below to tell him to let it fly. Antoninus understood: ask for his son to rule, and have his son free Tiberias. When Antoninus complained that important Romans were troubling him, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi took him to his garden and each day pulled up one radish in front of him. Antoninus understood: kill them one by one, and do not provoke them all at once.
18.why: The Gemara has said that the Romans do sometimes make a king's son king at the king's request, giving Asveirus son of Antoninus as the example. This story shows how that came about. Afterward the Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not simply speak openly.

people.name: Antoninus
people.about: A Roman emperor who seeks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's advice.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; answers Antoninus with silent demonstrations.

people.name: Asveirus
people.about: Antoninus' son, whom he wants to succeed him.

terms.meaning: A city in the Land of Israel.
Antoninus wants Tiberias exempted from paying taxes to Rome.

19.note: A Roman emperor who hated the Jews asked his nobles whether a man with a sore on his foot should cut it off and live, or leave it and suffer. They said cut it off. Ketia son of Shalom objected: the Jews can never all be destroyed, and Rome would be called the severed kingdom. The emperor agreed but said whoever defeats the king in argument is thrown into a furnace. As Ketia was led away, a noblewoman said: woe to the ship that sails without paying its tax. He circumcised himself and said he had paid his tax. As he was thrown in, he left all his property to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues. A Divine Voice declared Ketia destined for the World-to-Come, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi wept: some earn their world in one moment, others over many years.
19.why: A teaching reads the verse placing Edom's leaders in the netherworld as not including all its officers; the exception is Ketia son of Shalom. The Gemara asks who he was, and this story answers.

people.name: Ketia son of Shalom
people.about: A Roman official who argues against destroying the Jews and is put to death.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Receives Ketia's property with his colleagues and teaches how to divide it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; weeps when he hears the Divine Voice.

terms.meaning: Here a figure of speech for the Jewish people, whom the emperor wanted to remove.
A place of execution where a person was thrown to die.
A voice from Heaven announcing God's view.
The life after death promised to the righteous.

20.note: A woman came to Rav Hisda to confess. She said the lightest of her sins was that she had conceived her younger son with her older son. Rav Hisda said to prepare her burial shrouds, but she did not die.
20.why: The Gemara has read a verse in Proverbs as saying that people who turn back from heresy die. It asks whether that is always so, and brings this woman, whose worst sins implied heresy, as a case where it did not happen; she had not truly repented, it answers.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage to whom the woman confesses.

terms.meaning: The cloth garments a dead body is wrapped in; Rav Hisda is saying she will soon die.
Here, turning away from Jewish belief; the Gemara infers she had done this as well.
